chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Umar ibn Udhayna, from Zurara, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said:

Ten rak'at are — two rak'at from Zuhr, and two rak'at from Asr, and two rak'at of Subh, and two rak'at of Maghrib, and two rak'at of the later Isha. Doubt is not permissible in these, and whoever doubts in any of these must restart the prayer from the beginning.

These are the prayers which God — Mighty and Majestic — prescribed upon the believers in the Quran and delegated to Muhammad (peace be upon him and his family). Then the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family) added seven rak'at to the prayer, and these are the Sunnah in which there is no Quranic recitation — but rather glorification (tasbih), proclamation of God's oneness (tahlil), magnification (takbir), and supplication. Doubt can only occur in these.

So the Messenger of God (peace be upon him and his family) added to the prayer of the resident — not the traveler — two rak'at each in Zuhr, Asr, and the later Isha, and one rak'a in Maghrib for both the resident and the traveler.

key_terms.التفويض: Divine delegation/authorization; God delegated to the Prophet the authority to determine the sunnah additions to prayer
key_terms.المسافر: Traveler; entitled to shorten (qasr) the prayer
key_terms.المقيم: Resident; a person who is not traveling and must perform the full prayer
key_terms.الوهم: Doubt/error in the number of rak'at during prayer; a technical fiqh term for uncertainty during salat
key_terms.سنة: Prophetic practice; the additional seven rak'at established by the Prophet by delegation from God
key_terms.فرض: Divinely obligated; the ten rak'at were directly prescribed by God in the Quran

ai.seo_question: How many rak'at are obligatory in Islamic prayer according to Imam al-Baqir?
ai.summary: Imam al-Baqir (peace be upon him) explains the structure of the obligatory prayer: the original ten rak'at prescribed by God in the Quran, plus the seven additional rak'at added by the Prophet as Sunnah. This hadith establishes the doctrinal basis for why doubt in obligatory rak'at requires restarting the prayer, while doubt in the Sunnah rak'at does not. It also clarifies the traveler's shortened prayer — the resident performs seventeen rak'at total, while the traveler performs ten, both rooted in divine prescription and prophetic authority.
